name: Linux Fundamentals
summary: An operating system manages hardware and software and gives the user an interface to run programs. Linux is a free, open-source, multi-user and multitasking operating system built around the kernel + shell design.

sections.title: What an operating system does
points: An OS is a set of programs that controls the computer, manages hardware, and provides services to applications.
Main jobs: process management, memory management, file management, device management and security.
Types of OS: batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing (multitasking), real-time, distributed, network and embedded.
A batch system runs jobs without user interaction; a time-sharing system gives each user a small time slice.
A real-time OS guarantees a response within a fixed deadline (hard real-time or soft real-time).
Distributed OS looks like one system spread over many machines; a network OS lets hosts share resources.

sections.title: Linux architecture
points: Four main parts: hardware, kernel, shell and system utilities/applications.
Kernel is the core: it talks to the hardware and provides process, memory, device and file management.
Shell is the command interpreter between the user and the kernel (bash, sh, zsh, ksh).
System libraries and utilities are the programs that use the kernel services (ls, cp, ps).
Linux is a monolithic kernel: drivers can be built in or loaded as modules at runtime.
Everything in Linux is treated as a file: devices under /dev, running data under /proc.

sections.title: Kernel vs shell
points: Kernel runs in kernel (privileged) mode; user programs run in user mode and request actions with system calls.
Shell is a normal user program - it reads your command, expands it and asks the kernel to run it.
Shell does not print anything by itself; it starts programs like ls which write to the terminal.
Common system calls: fork (create process), exec (run program), open/read/write (files), wait (child).
A shell script is a file of shell commands executed in order.

sections.title: Boot process and runlevels
points: Boot order: BIOS/UEFI self-test -> bootloader (GRUB) -> kernel loaded into memory -> initramfs -> root filesystem mount.
The kernel starts PID 1, which is systemd on modern Linux (init on older systems).
systemd starts units (services, mounts, targets); older SysV used runlevels 0-6.
Runlevel 0 = halt, 1 = single-user, 2 = multi-user without network, 3 = full text multi-user, 5 = graphical, 6 = reboot.
Runlevel 4 is normally unused; systemctl get-default shows the current default target.
GRUB menu configuration is /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (or /boot/grub/grub.conf on older Red Hat).

sections.title: Important Linux facts
points: Linux is case-sensitive: File, file and FILE are three different names.
A normal user's UID starts at 1000; root always has UID 0.
The superuser (root) can do everything; normal users need sudo for privileged commands.
Linux file extensions do not control the file type; the file command reads the content instead.
Standard input/stdout/stderr are file descriptors 0, 1 and 2.

name: Process Management and Scheduling
summary: A process is a program in execution with its own memory, state and process control block (PCB). The scheduler decides which ready process gets the CPU next.

sections.title: Process basics
points: Program = passive file on disk; process = active copy in memory with PID and state.
The PCB stores PID, program counter, CPU registers, memory limits, open files and scheduling information.
Process states: new, ready, running, waiting (blocked), terminated.
A running process becomes waiting when it asks for I/O and becomes ready when the I/O completes.
Context switch saves the old process state and loads the new process state; it has overhead.
A thread is a lightweight process sharing code, data and files, but each thread has its own stack and registers.
Zombie = finished child not yet reaped by parent; orphan = child whose parent already exited.

sections.title: Schedulers
points: Long-term scheduler admits jobs from the job pool into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming.
Short-term (CPU) scheduler picks the next ready process for the CPU - it runs very often.
Medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and brings them back later (reduce thrashing).
FCFS is simple but causes the convoy effect (short jobs wait behind a long job).
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time but starvation is possible; SRTF is its preemptive version.
Priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs - aging gradually raises their priority.
Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum and is good for time-sharing systems.
Multilevel queue uses fixed queues (foreground/background); multilevel feedback queue moves processes between queues.

sections.title: Scheduling criteria
points: CPU utilization should be as high as possible.
Throughput = number of processes completed per unit time.
Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time.
Waiting time = total time spent in the ready queue.
Response time = time from submission to the first response (important for interactive systems).
A fair scheduler ensures no process waits forever (no starvation).

sections.title: Inter-process communication (IPC)
points: Pipe allows related processes to communicate; FIFO (named pipe) works between unrelated processes.
Message passing and shared memory are the two main IPC models.
Semaphores protect shared memory and provide synchronisation (wait/signal).
Classic problems: producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers.
A socket is used for communication across the network (TCP/UDP).
Signals (kill) are software interrupts sent to a process.

sections.title: Linux process commands
points: ps aux shows all running processes; top/htop shows them live with CPU and memory usage.
kill -9 PID forces termination; kill -15 (default) asks the process to stop cleanly.
nice and renice change process priority (-20 highest priority, 19 lowest; ordinary users can only increase nice value).
jobs, bg and fg manage background and foreground shell jobs.
pstree shows the process tree; pgrep finds a PID by process name.

name: Memory Management
summary: The OS allocates and frees memory for processes, gives each process a virtual address space, and uses paging and swapping to run programs bigger than RAM.

sections.title: Allocation basics
points: In contiguous allocation each process gets one continuous block of memory.
Fragmentation: internal waste inside an allocated block, external waste as small free holes.
First Fit takes the first hole big enough; Best Fit takes the smallest hole big enough; Worst Fit takes the largest hole.
Compaction reduces external fragmentation but is expensive (shuffles memory).
Swapping moves a whole process out to disk when memory is full.

sections.title: Paging and segmentation
points: Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size.
Page table maps page number to frame number; the TLB caches recent page-table entries.
Paging removes external fragmentation but can have internal fragmentation in the last page.
Segmentation divides a program into variable-size logical segments (code, stack, data).
Segmentation can cause external fragmentation; paging does not support logical grouping.
In a virtual memory system the page tables and segmentation tables are kept in RAM.

sections.title: Virtual memory and page faults
points: Virtual memory gives an illusion of a very large main memory using disk as a backing store.
Demand paging loads a page only when it is referenced; a page fault occurs when it is not in memory.
Page replacement algorithms decide which page to remove: FIFO, LRU and Optimal.
FIFO can suffer from Belady's anomaly (more frames = more faults); LRU and Optimal do not.
Optimal replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time (not practical, used for comparison).
Thrashing is excessive paging - the system spends more time swapping than executing.

sections.title: Details worth remembering
points: Locality of reference (temporal and spatial) is why cache memory works.
With 3 frames and a reference string, count faults with FIFO versus LRU for practice questions.
Swap size for small RAM systems is commonly 1-2 times RAM; a 128 MB workstation needs roughly 100-256 MB swap.
free -h, vmstat and /proc/meminfo show memory use on Linux.
A memory leak slowly reduces available memory because the program never frees it.
32-bit Linux normally supports up to 4 GB of virtual address space per process.

name: Linux File System and Permissions
summary: Linux uses a single directory tree starting at /. Files have owners, groups and rwx permissions, plus special bits such as setuid, setgid and sticky.

sections.title: Directory layout (FHS)
points: / is the root; /bin and /usr/bin hold commands; /sbin holds administrator commands.
/etc holds configuration files; /home holds user home directories; /root is root's home.
/var holds variable data such as logs and mail (/var/log, /var/spool/mail).
/tmp is temporary space and has the sticky bit set.
/dev holds device files; /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel data.
/usr contains programs and libraries; /opt holds add-on software.
A hidden file starts with a dot (.bashrc); ls -a shows hidden files.

sections.title: Files, inodes and links
points: Every file has an inode that stores type, owner, group, permissions, size, timestamps and data block pointers.
The directory maps names to inode numbers.
Hard link: another name for the same inode (ln file1 file2); it shares data and inode number.
Symbolic (soft) link: a separate small file that points to a path (ln -s target link).
A hard link cannot cross filesystems and cannot point to a directory; a symbolic link can.
Absolute path starts from /; relative path starts from the current directory.

sections.title: Permissions
points: Permissions are read (r=4), write (w=2) and execute (x=1) for user, group and others.
chmod 755 file means rwxr-xr-x; chmod u+x file adds execute for the owner.
chown changes the owner and chgrp changes the group.
umask 022 gives new files 644 and new directories 755 (defaults minus umask).
Special bits: setuid (4000) runs a file as its owner, setgid (2000) runs with the group or keeps a directory group.
Sticky bit (1000) on a directory lets only the owner delete files - use chmod o+t /tmp or chmod 1777.
An ACL gives finer permissions: getfacl shows it and setfacl -m u:user:rwx file adds an entry.

sections.title: Disks, mounts and filesystems
points: Common filesystems: ext3, ext4 and xfs; ext4 is the default on modern Red Hat and Debian.
mkfs creates a filesystem, mount attaches it to the tree, umount detaches it.
/etc/fstab stores permanent mounts; blkid and lsblk show device information.
df -h shows free space per filesystem; du -sh directory shows size of a directory.
fsck checks and repairs a filesystem - run it on an unmounted filesystem.
A swap partition normally has filesystem ID 82.
LVM uses physical volumes (PV), volume groups (VG) and logical volumes (LV); default extent size is 4 MB.

name: Linux Commands, Redirection and Regex
summary: Most Linux admin work is done from the shell. Important skills are file commands, viewing text, redirection and pipes, regular expressions, vi and cron.

sections.title: File and text commands
points: ls -l lists details, ls -la includes hidden files, ls -R lists recursively.
cp, mv, rm, mkdir, rmdir, touch create or remove files and directories.
find searches by name, size, time or permissions (find / -name '*.log'), locate uses a database index.
cat prints a file, less pages through it, head/tail show the beginning/end, tail -f follows a growing file.
grep searches text (-i ignore case, -r recursive, -v invert match).
wc counts lines, words and characters; sort sorts; uniq removes adjacent duplicates; cut takes columns.
tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir creates an archive; tar -xzf extracts; gzip/bzip2 compress single files.

sections.title: Redirection and pipes
points: > writes stdout to a file (overwrites); >> appends.
< takes stdin from a file.
2> redirects stderr; 2>&1 sends stderr to the same place as stdout; &> redirects both.
| connects the stdout of one command to the stdin of the next (ps aux | grep sshd).
tee writes output to a file and also shows it on the screen.
No output from a command means it succeeded with empty stdout.
* matches any characters, ? matches one character, [abc] matches a set.

sections.title: Regular expressions
points: ^ matches the start of a line, $ matches the end.
. matches any one character; * means zero or more of the previous item; + means one or more (grep -E).
[0-9] is a character class; [^0-9] means not a digit.
{n,m} means between n and m repetitions (extended regex).
\b is a word boundary; () groups and | means OR in extended regex.
grep -E uses extended regex; sed replaces text (sed 's/old/new/g' file).
awk is a field-based text processor (awk '{print $1}' file).

sections.title: vi editor and cron
points: vi modes: command mode (Esc), insert mode (i/a/o), last-line mode (:).
Save and quit: :w writes, :q quits, :wq or ZZ saves and quits, :q! quits without saving.
Delete, copy, paste: dd deletes a line, yy copies a line, p pastes, x deletes a character.
Navigation: h j k l move left/down/up/right; /word searches forward.
crontab -e edits the schedule; crontab -l lists it; the five fields are minute hour day month weekday.
30 4 * * 3 runs at 04:30 every Wednesday (weekly).
* means every value; */5 means every 5 units; @reboot runs at startup.

name: Users, Groups and System Monitoring
summary: Linux keeps user and group accounts in text files and uses them to decide who can do what. Monitoring tools and logs show what the system is doing.

sections.title: Account files and commands
points: /etc/passwd holds user name, UID, GID, home directory and shell (no password).
/etc/shadow holds the password hash and aging information - readable only by root.
/etc/group lists groups and member users; /etc/gshadow stores group passwords.
useradd creates a user, usermod changes one, userdel removes one; passwd sets the password.
id shows UID, GID and all groups; groups username lists group membership.
usermod -L user locks an account; usermod -U unlocks it; chage manages password expiry.
su switches user; sudo runs one command as root and is logged.
An administrator can lock a user account so the password cannot be used.

sections.title: Monitoring performance
points: ps aux lists processes; top/htop shows live CPU, memory and load.
uptime shows load average for 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
free -h shows RAM and swap; vmstat shows memory, swap and CPU statistics.
iostat shows disk I/O; netstat -tulpn or ss -tulpn show listening ports.
lsof lists open files and the processes using them.
dmesg shows kernel messages (hardware, drivers); journalctl reads the systemd journal.

sections.title: Logs
points: /var/log/messages holds general system messages on Red Hat systems.
/var/log/secure (Red Hat) or /var/log/auth.log (Debian) records authentication and sudo events.
/var/log/dmesg holds boot-time kernel messages.
rsyslog writes logs by facility and priority; logrotate prevents logs from filling the disk.
A daemon's messages normally go to /var/log/messages, not to a file named after the daemon.
journalctl -u service shows the log for one systemd unit.

sections.title: Network configuration
points: ip addr / ifconfig show interfaces; ip route shows the routing table.
Red Hat stores interface config in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0.
/etc/resolv.conf sets DNS servers; /etc/hosts is a local static name table.
/etc/nsswitch.conf sets the order of name lookups (files, dns, nis).
/etc/services maps port numbers to service names.
systemctl restart network (or NetworkManager) applies network changes.

name: Shell Scripting
summary: A shell script is a text file of shell commands and logic. Scripts automate backups, monitoring, user creation and mail processing.

sections.title: Script basics
points: Start with #!/bin/bash (the shebang) so the kernel knows which shell to use.
Make the script executable with chmod +x script.sh, then run ./script.sh.
# starts a comment; comments explain the script and are ignored at runtime.
Variables: name=value (no spaces around =); read it with $name or ${name}.
Quotes: double quotes allow variable expansion, single quotes do not.
Command substitution: now=$(date) stores the output of a command.
Arithmetic: sum=$((a + b)).

sections.title: Operators and tests
points: Arithmetic operators: + - * / % and ** for power (inside $(( ))).
Relational operators for numbers: -eq, -ne, -gt, -lt, -ge, -le.
String tests: =, !=, -z (empty), -n (not empty).
File tests: -e exists, -f regular file, -d directory, -r readable, -w writable, -x executable, -s non-empty.
Boolean operators: && (and), || (or), ! (not).
test condition is same as [ condition ]; [[ ]] is the safer bash version.

sections.title: Control structures
points: if [ condition ]; then ... elif ...; else ...; fi.
case $value in pattern) ... ;; *) ... ;; esac.
for i in 1 2 3; do ...; done or for file in *.log.
while [ condition ]; do ...; done runs while true; until runs until true.
break exits the loop, continue jumps to the next iteration.
exit N returns a status code: 0 means success, non-zero means failure.
$? is the exit status of the last command.

sections.title: Functions and arguments
points: Function: name() { commands; } and call it as name.
$0 is the script name, $1..$9 are arguments, $# is the argument count.
$@ is all arguments as separate words; $* is all arguments as one string.
$$ is the current process id; $! is the last background process id.
Local variables inside functions use the local keyword.
Final line of a script should normally be exit 0.

sections.title: Practical patterns
points: Backup script: date stamp, tar -czf /backup/home-$(date +%F).tar.gz /home, check exit code.
Log cleanup: find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete.
Menu script: read choice, then case statement to call functions.
Check a service: systemctl is-active sshd || systemctl start sshd.
Schedule a script with cron (for example 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh).
Write errors to a file: command 2>> /var/log/script.err.

name: Linux Administration and Servers
summary: Linux administration covers services, SSH, disks, network settings and common servers such as a mail server. systemd manages services on modern distributions.

sections.title: Service management
points: systemctl start/stop/restart/status service controls a service.
systemctl enable service starts it at boot; disable removes it from boot.
systemctl list-units --type=service lists running services.
Old SysV commands: service name start and chkconfig --list for runlevels.
Enable a service now with service name start; chkconfig only affects boot behaviour.
journalctl -u name shows the service log.

sections.title: Secure SSH
points: sshd listens on TCP 22 and is configured in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
Key-based login: ssh-keygen makes a key pair; the public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Disable direct root login (PermitRootLogin no) and prefer SSH keys over passwords.
Change the default port and restrict users with AllowUsers for extra safety.
scp and sftp copy files securely over SSH; ssh -L creates a local tunnel.
ssh connects to a remote shell with an encrypted tunnel; Telnet and rlogin send clear text.

sections.title: Disk and network administration
points: fdisk -l lists disks; fdisk /dev/sdb partitions a new disk.
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1 builds the filesystem, mount attaches it, and /etc/fstab makes it permanent.
LVM: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend plus resize2fs to grow a filesystem.
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0 sets an address; ip link set eth0 up enables the interface.
The default gateway is the router interface on the local network.
firewall: iptables or firewalld (firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent).
ntp/chronyd keeps the clock correct; timedatectl shows time settings.

sections.title: Mail server basics
points: MUA (mail client) -> MTA (postfix/sendmail) -> MDA (delivery) -> mailbox -> MRA (dovecot) for IMAP/POP3.
Sendmail/postfix are MTAs; dovecot is an IMAP/POP3 server; Thunderbird is an MUA.
Postfix main configuration is /etc/postfix/main.cf.
SMTP uses port 25 (server to server), 587 (submission with auth); POP3 110, IMAP 143, secure 993/995.
Mailboxes are stored in /var/spool/mail/<user> for mbox format.
A user forwards mail with a ~/.forward file; /etc/aliases changes delivery for everyone.
Mail queue commands: postqueue -p to view and postqueue -f to flush.

sections.title: Other common services
points: BIND (named) is the DNS server; its zone files live in /var/named and config in /etc/named.conf.
Apache (httpd) main config is /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf; DocumentRoot is /var/www/html.
NFS shares directories listed in /etc/exports; the client mounts server:/share.
Samba shares files and printers with Windows using SMB/CIFS.
Squid proxy default port is 3128 and config is /etc/squid/squid.conf.
NTP server uses UDP 123; DNS uses 53; DHCP uses 67/68.
